medium.titulo: I Found the Most Creative Ways People Use Claude (And Some Are Surprisingly Useful)
medium.resumo: Most people open Claude, type a question, get an answer, and close the tab.
medium.conteudo_html:
Most people open Claude, type a question, get an answer, and close the tab.

Some use it to write emails. Others ask it to summarise documents, generate code, or help with research.

But there’s another side of Claude that is much more interesting.

People are experimenting with ways to turn it into a video editor, personal assistant, business automation system, app builder, data analyst, and even a tool for understanding their everyday lives.

Some of these ideas sound like something you’d expect from a dedicated software product rather than an AI assistant.

Imagine asking Claude to turn your WhatsApp conversations into something useful, build an interactive 3D version of your IKEA manual, organise thousands of family photographs, or transform meeting notes into a business proposal.

That’s where things get interesting.

I went through a collection of creative Claude workflows and use cases, and what stood out wasn’t just the technology. It was how differently people are thinking about AI.

Instead of asking, “What can Claude tell me?”, they’re beginning to ask, “What can Claude actually do for me?”

Here are some of the most interesting ways people are experimenting with it.

1. Turn Claude into a video editing assistant

Video editing can consume hours, especially when you’re working with long recordings, podcasts, interviews, or social media content.

AI-powered editing workflows are changing how creators approach this work.

With specialised skills and video-editing integrations, Claude can help organise the process, identify interesting sections, prepare clips, and assist with content repurposing.

Think about a two-hour podcast.

Instead of manually watching the entire recording to find interesting moments, you could build a workflow that:

  • Identifies potentially valuable sections.
  • Extracts timestamps and memorable statements.
  • Suggests short-form video clips.
  • Creates captions and social media descriptions.
  • Organises the output for different platforms.

Tools such as OpusClip can complement this workflow by handling video-specific editing and clipping.

The interesting part is connecting these capabilities into one repeatable content production process.

2. Use Claude to interact with WhatsApp

What if you could use an AI assistant to help manage everyday messaging?

Imagine asking Claude to prepare a response to someone, summarise an important conversation, or organise information from your messages.

For example:

  • Draft a professional reply.
  • Summarise a long conversation.
  • Extract important dates and commitments.
  • Turn a discussion into a task list.
  • Prepare follow-up messages.

With an appropriate WhatsApp integration or automation platform, some of these workflows can become more than simple text generation.

There is one important distinction: Claude does not automatically have access to your WhatsApp account. You need an authorised integration or an automation layer, and messages should be reviewed before sending.

Still, the possibility of having an assistant help manage communication is worth exploring.

3. Ask Claude to read contracts and terms and conditions

Let’s be honest. Most people don’t read every line of a 30-page agreement.

We scroll through the document, look for the important parts, and sometimes accept conditions without understanding what we’re agreeing to.

Claude can help make these documents easier to understand.

Upload a contract or terms and conditions document and ask it to identify:

  • Payment obligations.
  • Cancellation policies.
  • Renewal conditions.
  • Hidden or unexpected charges.
  • Termination clauses.
  • Confidentiality requirements.
  • Important deadlines.

You can also ask it to explain complicated legal language in plain English.

A useful prompt:

“Review this agreement and create a summary of the most important obligations, potential risks, cancellation conditions, and financial commitments. Highlight anything that requires additional attention.”

This is particularly useful before signing service agreements, subscriptions, freelance contracts, or business partnerships.

However, an AI-generated review is not a substitute for professional legal advice. Have a qualified lawyer review important agreements.

4. Let Claude automate your content workflow

Content creators spend a surprising amount of time doing things that aren’t actually writing.

Researching topics, preparing outlines, creating social media captions, repurposing articles, organising ideas, and maintaining a publishing schedule all require attention.

Claude can help connect these activities into a more structured workflow.

For example, you could create a content production system that:

  1. Collects ideas from a topic database.
  2. Researches a selected subject.
  3. Prepares an article outline.
  4. Creates a first draft.
  5. Generates LinkedIn and X variations.
  6. Prepares newsletter introductions.
  7. Organises everything into a content calendar.

You can also connect Claude with tools such as Google Drive, Notion, or automation platforms to move information between applications.

The real benefit isn’t generating 100 posts in one day.

It’s reducing the repetitive work between having an idea and publishing something valuable.

5. Find possible refunds with Claude

This is one of the more practical ideas.

People often forget about subscriptions, duplicate payments, unexpected charges, or purchases that might qualify for a refund.

Claude can help review receipts, invoices, subscription terms, and refund policies.

You could provide the relevant documents and ask it to:

  • Identify possible duplicate charges.
  • Find refund eligibility conditions.
  • Calculate relevant refund deadlines.
  • Summarise cancellation requirements.
  • Draft a customer support message.

For example:

“Review these purchase receipts and the refund policy. Identify transactions that may qualify for a refund and draft a separate support request for each eligible transaction.”

It won’t guarantee a refund or independently reverse a payment. But it can help you understand the situation and prepare a clearer request.

6. Turn meeting notes into proposals and contracts

Meetings generate ideas, decisions, commitments, and action items.

Unfortunately, a lot of that information gets buried in notes.

Claude can help turn unstructured meeting notes into professional business documents.

Imagine finishing a client meeting and having a document containing:

  • Project requirements.
  • Scope of work.
  • Deliverables.
  • Pricing discussions.
  • Estimated timelines.
  • Responsibilities.
  • Next steps.

You can ask Claude to convert those notes into a structured proposal.

From there, it can help prepare a contract draft based on the agreed terms.

This is particularly useful for freelancers, consultants, agencies, and small business owners.

Instead of starting every proposal from a blank document, you have a repeatable process.

Always verify the commercial terms and obtain appropriate legal review before sending a contract for signature.

7. Build your own language-learning application

You don’t necessarily need to start with a large development team to experiment with building a language-learning application.

Claude can help you design and develop a basic application around your learning requirements.

Imagine an app that includes:

  • Daily vocabulary exercises.
  • Grammar explanations.
  • Interactive quizzes.
  • Sentence correction.
  • Progress tracking.
  • Personalised practice sessions.
  • Conversation exercises.

You could ask Claude to build a simple interface, generate the application code, explain the implementation, and help debug problems.

With additional integrations for speech recognition and text-to-speech, you could explore pronunciation and speaking exercises too.

The exciting part is that you can build something around your own learning style instead of adapting completely to an existing application.

8. Turn your conversations into a personal dashboard

We generate a lot of information through everyday conversations.

Some contain business ideas. Others contain personal goals, project decisions, reminders, or recurring problems.

Instead of allowing everything to remain scattered across chat histories, you could export selected conversations and ask Claude to organise them.

For example, it could help create a dashboard showing:

  • Frequently discussed topics.
  • Ongoing projects.
  • Repeated questions.
  • Important decisions.
  • Unfinished tasks.
  • Business ideas.
  • Personal learning goals.

You could even build a simple dashboard using a spreadsheet or web application.

One interesting application is identifying patterns in your own thinking.

What projects do you repeatedly return to? Which ideas never move beyond the planning stage? What tasks keep appearing?

The dashboard becomes a way to review your activity rather than simply storing conversations.

Be mindful of sensitive information when exporting or processing private conversations.

9. Turn boring appliance manuals into interactive 3D experiences

This is one of the most creative ideas on the list.

Think about buying a new appliance or assembling IKEA furniture.

You receive a manual containing diagrams, numbered instructions, and technical descriptions.

Sometimes understanding a single assembly step takes longer than actually completing it.

What if you could turn those instructions into an interactive experience?

With Claude assisting with document interpretation and application development, you could experiment with an application that:

  • Extracts assembly instructions.
  • Organises individual steps.
  • Displays relevant diagrams.
  • Creates interactive checklists.
  • Presents 3D models where suitable assets are available.
  • Explains complicated assembly steps.

Imagine rotating a furniture component, selecting a part, and understanding exactly where it belongs.

The important distinction is that Claude does not automatically transform every manual into an accurate 3D model. That requires suitable model assets, 3D tooling, and validation.

But as an application-building experiment, this is genuinely interesting.

10. Create new outfits from clothes you already own

Most people have more clothes than they regularly wear.

The problem isn’t always a lack of options. Sometimes it’s a lack of ideas.

You could use Claude to help build a personal wardrobe assistant.

Start by organising photographs of your existing clothes.

Then ask it to help:

  • Categorise clothing items.
  • Identify colours and clothing types.
  • Suggest outfit combinations.
  • Create looks for different occasions.
  • Recommend combinations based on weather or dress codes.
  • Build a wardrobe inventory.

For example, you could ask:

“Using these wardrobe photographs, suggest five casual outfits for a weekend trip. Avoid repeating the same combination and prioritise clothes that work together.”

With image understanding and an appropriate application interface, this could become a useful personal styling tool.

11. Organise family and travel photographs automatically

Thousands of photographs can become difficult to manage.

You might have pictures from family events, vacations, birthdays, and different locations scattered across multiple folders.

Claude can help design a photo-organisation workflow that categorises images using available metadata and image recognition tools.

Possible categories include:

  • Locations.
  • Travel destinations.
  • Activities.
  • Family events.
  • Dates and occasions.
  • Recognised people, where supported and appropriate.

You could build a searchable photo dashboard where you can find pictures by asking questions such as:

“Show me the photographs from my last beach vacation.”

Or:

“Find pictures from family celebrations in 2025.”

This workflow requires access to the photo library and suitable image-processing capabilities. Face recognition also raises privacy considerations, particularly when organizing photographs of other people.

12. Recover data from a corrupted hard drive

Losing access to important files is frustrating, especially when they contain work documents, photographs, or personal projects.

Claude can help explain recovery options, troubleshoot errors, and guide users through safer diagnostic steps.

You could share error messages, operating system information, and details about the drive to get help understanding possible causes.

It can also help you:

  • Identify common file-system problems.
  • Understand recovery software options.
  • Prepare diagnostic commands.
  • Interpret recovery logs.
  • Plan a backup strategy.

One important warning: if a drive is physically failing, stop using it and avoid running repair commands that could make data loss worse. A professional recovery service may be the safest option.

Claude cannot guarantee recovery of corrupted or physically damaged storage.

13. Explore the Last 30 Days skill

Another interesting concept is using a specialised skill to review activity over a defined period.

A Last 30 Days workflow could help turn scattered information into a monthly review.

For example, you could use it to organise:

  • Completed projects.
  • Important conversations.
  • Research activity.
  • Unfinished tasks.
  • Recurring themes.
  • Upcoming priorities.

Rather than simply asking what happened during the previous month, you could build a structured report showing what changed and what needs attention.

The usefulness depends on what information sources the skill can actually access.

14. Build your own photo-editing application

Instead of relying entirely on existing photo-editing software, you can experiment with building a lightweight editing application using Claude.

Start with a few basic features:

  • Image cropping.
  • Brightness and contrast adjustment.
  • Filters.
  • Background removal through an appropriate integration.
  • Image resizing.
  • Text overlays.
  • Export options.

Claude can help write the code, design the interface, and connect image-processing libraries or APIs.

For developers, this is an interesting way to learn how image-editing applications work.

For creators, it could become a small tool built around a specific editing workflow.

15. Turn health data into dashboards and insights

Health information can be difficult to understand when it is scattered across different applications.

With properly authorised data exports and integrations, Claude can help organise information into a more readable dashboard.

For example, you could explore visualising:

  • Daily activity.
  • Sleep patterns.
  • Exercise frequency.
  • Meal records.
  • Fitness progress.
  • Personal goals.

You could then ask questions about trends in the information.

For instance:

“Summarise my activity over the last month and identify changes in my exercise consistency.”

Or:

“Organise my meal records into a weekly dashboard.”

This can make personal tracking easier, but health data is sensitive. Use trusted integrations, limit unnecessary sharing, and don’t treat AI-generated observations as medical diagnoses or treatment recommendations.

16. Clip long podcasts and search through them

Podcasts contain useful information, but finding a particular discussion inside a two-hour episode can be difficult.

A transcription and search workflow can make that information much easier to access.

Claude can help analyse transcripts, identify topics, and locate relevant sections.

A practical system could:

  1. Transcribe the audio.
  2. Divide it into searchable sections.
  3. Identify important discussions.
  4. Extract useful quotations.
  5. Generate timestamps.
  6. Prepare short summaries.
  7. Suggest clips for social media.

You could even create a searchable personal podcast library.

Instead of remembering which episode discussed a particular business idea, you could search across your transcripts.

17. Turn Claude into a sales assistant

Sales teams spend a lot of time researching prospects, preparing messages, following up, and updating customer records.

Claude can help organise these activities into a more efficient process.

For example:

  • Research potential customers using authorised information sources.
  • Prepare personalised outreach drafts.
  • Summarise previous customer conversations.
  • Identify unanswered questions.
  • Prepare follow-up messages.
  • Draft sales proposals.
  • Organise lead information.

When connected to a CRM and automation tools, some of these activities can become part of a repeatable sales workflow.

The goal shouldn’t be to send thousands of generic AI-generated messages.

It should be to help salespeople spend more time understanding potential customers and less time handling repetitive administration.

18. Clear disk space and Google Drive storage

Running out of storage is a familiar problem.

Old downloads, duplicate files, unused documents, large videos, and forgotten folders can accumulate over time.

Claude can help build a storage-cleanup assistant that analyses file information and identifies potential cleanup opportunities.

It could:

  • Find large files.
  • Identify duplicate candidates.
  • Categorise downloads.
  • Locate old folders.
  • Generate storage reports.
  • Suggest files for archiving.

For Google Drive, an authorised integration can help organise and review files.

For local storage, a script or desktop application can perform the analysis.

Always review proposed deletions before removing anything. An AI-generated cleanup recommendation should never automatically mean a file is safe to delete.

19. Turn an old phone or monitor into a home display

Have an old smartphone or monitor sitting unused?

You could repurpose it as a simple home information display.

With Claude helping develop the application, you could create a dashboard showing:

  • Weather information.
  • Calendar events.
  • Daily reminders.
  • Tasks.
  • Family schedules.
  • News headlines.
  • Personal productivity information.

An old phone could function as a compact display on your desk, while a larger monitor could become a household information screen.

This is also a fun beginner development project because you can experiment with web dashboards, APIs, responsive design, and scheduled data updates.

20. Experiment with specialised Claude skills and creative projects

Beyond everyday tasks, there are interesting opportunities to explore specialised skills and experimental projects.

The reference collection also points toward names and ideas such as REA, Lemo, an Opuscar video-editing skill, Zero to Infinity with AI, and Hack Your TV.

These are worth exploring as individual experiments rather than assuming they are all native Claude features.

The broader idea is what matters: specialised workflows can extend an AI assistant into activities that would otherwise require several separate applications.

A skill can give Claude a defined set of instructions, while integrations and external tools can provide additional capabilities.

That combination is where many of the more unusual experiments begin.

What Makes These Claude Use Cases Interesting?

Looking at these examples, one thing becomes clear: the most interesting ways people are using Claude aren’t simply about writing better prompts or getting faster answers. They’re about changing how we interact with everyday software.

Instead of handling every task manually, people are finding ways to make AI part of the process.

For example:

  • Contract reviews: Instead of reading lengthy contracts line by line, use AI to identify important clauses, highlight potential risks, and summarise key obligations.
  • Video editing: Rather than manually searching through hours of footage, use AI to find relevant moments and prepare shorter clips.
  • Proposal creation: Instead of starting from a blank document, turn meeting notes and discussions into structured proposal drafts.
  • Photo organisation: Rather than searching through thousands of images one by one, use image analysis and metadata to organise photos by location, activity, or other details.
  • Personal dashboards: Instead of manually tracking different activities, bring available data together to create dashboards and uncover useful patterns.
  • Interactive manuals: Rather than struggling through complicated appliance or IKEA instructions, turn them into interactive guides that make each step easier to understand.
  • Content management: Instead of switching between multiple tools for research, writing, editing, and publishing, connect these activities into a more organised workflow.

The bigger shift is not just that AI can answer questions. It’s that AI can help connect different tasks, tools, and decisions into a workflow.

We’re moving from using AI as a place to ask questions to using it as a layer that helps us get work done.

But there is an important distinction: not every workflow is fully autonomous, and not every task should be handed over to AI without supervision.

But there is an important distinction.

Claude is not automatically all these tools in one application.

Some workflows require Claude skills, integrations, APIs, external software, custom code, or automation platforms.

Some require human approval before taking action.

And some are still experiments rather than polished, ready-to-use products.

Understanding that distinction is important. Otherwise, it’s easy to confuse an interesting demonstration with a reliable tool you can use every day.

The bigger opportunity isn’t using AI. It’s building with it.

The most interesting thing about these experiments isn’t any individual feature.

It’s the way people are starting to approach problems.

A creator doesn’t necessarily need another content application. They might need a workflow that connects research, writing, editing, and publishing.

A small business owner doesn’t necessarily need another CRM feature. They might need a system that turns customer conversations into proposals and follow-ups.

Someone trying to organise their personal life doesn’t necessarily need another productivity application. They might need a dashboard that brings their existing information together.

That’s a different way of thinking about AI.

Instead of asking which AI tool is the most powerful, start by identifying a repetitive task, a frustrating process, or information that is difficult to organise.

Then ask:

Can I build a workflow that makes this easier?

You might discover that the best AI application for your needs isn’t something you download.

It’s something you create.

Final thoughts

Claude is interesting because it can be used in so many different ways.

From turning meeting notes into business documents to experimenting with interactive applications, personal dashboards, video workflows, and everyday automation, the possibilities extend well beyond ordinary conversations.

But the real value isn’t in collecting dozens of AI tools.

It’s in finding one problem that takes too much time and figuring out how to solve it better.

That’s where I’d start.

medium.resumo: Modern web development is not just about writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
medium.conteudo_html:
Modern web development is not just about writing HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.

Today’s applications need dynamic interfaces, reusable components, reactive data, and efficient ways to manage user interactions.

This is where Vue.js comes in.

Vue.js is a progressive JavaScript framework used to build user interfaces and single-page applications. It is beginner-friendly, flexible, and powerful enough for large-scale applications.

If you are starting with Vue.js or want to strengthen your JavaScript frontend fundamentals, this guide will help you understand the core concepts with practical examples.

Let’s get started!

1. What Is Vue.js?

Vue.js is an open-source JavaScript framework for building user interfaces.

It allows developers to create dynamic applications by connecting JavaScript data with HTML templates.

For example, imagine you have a counter application.

With plain JavaScript, you need to manually find an HTML element and update its content whenever the value changes.

With Vue.js, you simply connect the data to the template. When the data changes, Vue automatically updates the interface.

Why Do Developers Use Vue.js?

  • Easy to learn and understand.
  • Component-based architecture.
  • Reactive data management.
  • Reusable UI components.
  • Flexible integration with existing projects.
  • Excellent ecosystem for modern frontend development.

Vue is commonly used for dashboards, admin panels, e-commerce applications, SaaS platforms, and interactive web applications.

2. Understanding the Vue Project Structure

Before writing Vue code, let’s understand how a typical Vue 3 project is organized.

A common project structure looks like this:

my-vue-app/
│
├── public/
│
├── src/
│   ├── assets/
│   ├── components/
│   ├── views/
│   ├── router/
│   ├── App.vue
│   └── main.js
│
├── index.html
├── package.json
└── vite.config.js

Here is what these files and folders do:

  • components/ — Stores reusable Vue components.
  • views/ — Stores page-level components.
  • assets/ — Contains images, styles, and other assets.
  • router/ — Contains application routing configuration.
  • App.vue — The root Vue component.
  • main.js — The application entry point.
  • package.json — Manages project dependencies and scripts.

Vue applications commonly use Single File Components with the .vue extension.

3. Understanding Vue Single File Components (SFC)

A Vue Single File Component allows you to organize HTML, JavaScript, and CSS in one file.

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const message = ref('Hello Vue.js!')
</script>
<template>
    <h1>{{ message }}</h1>
</template>
<style scoped>
h1 {
    color: #42b883;
}
</style>

A Vue component usually contains three main sections:

Script: Handles JavaScript logic and data.

Template: Defines the HTML structure of the component.

Style: Contains component-specific CSS.

The scoped attribute ensures that the component's styles are scoped to that component.

The script setup syntax is a convenient way to write Composition API code in Vue 3.

4. Understanding Reactivity in Vue.js

Reactivity is one of the most important concepts in Vue.

It means that when application data changes, Vue automatically updates the relevant parts of the user interface.

Let’s understand this with an example.

Using ref()

The ref() function creates a reactive reference.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const increment = () => {
    count.value++
}
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Count: {{ count }}</h2>
    <button @click="increment">
        Increase
    </button>
</template>

Here:

  • ref(0) creates a reactive value.
  • count.value accesses or updates the value in JavaScript.
  • {{ count }} displays the value in the template.
  • @click listens for button clicks.

An interesting detail: inside JavaScript, you access a ref using .value. In Vue templates, top-level refs are automatically unwrapped.

Using reactive()

Vue also provides reactive() to create reactive objects.

<script setup>
import { reactive } from 'vue'

const user = reactive({
    name: 'Jalis',
    role: 'Developer',
    experience: 4
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>{{ user.name }}</h2>
    <p>{{ user.role }}</p>
    <p>{{ user.experience }} Years Experience</p>
</template>

The main difference:

ref()reactive()Works with primitive values and objectsDesigned for objectsAccess value using .value in JavaScriptAccess properties directlyCan be reassigned as a referenceCannot be replaced as a whole while retaining the original reactive connection

Developer Tip: Use ref() for most reactive state, especially when you need to replace the value. Use reactive() when working with a reactive object.

5. Understanding Vue Directives

Directives are special Vue attributes that add reactive behavior to HTML elements.

Some important Vue directives include:

A. v-if

v-if conditionally renders an element.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const isLoggedIn = ref(true)
</script>
<template>
    <h2 v-if="isLoggedIn">
        Welcome Back!
    </h2>
    <h2 v-else>
        Please Login
    </h2>
</template>

If isLoggedIn is true, the first heading appears.

Otherwise, Vue renders the second heading.

B. v-show

v-show controls an element's visibility using CSS.

<template>
    <h2 v-show="isLoggedIn">
        Welcome Back!
    </h2>
</template>

Unlike v-if, v-show keeps the element in the DOM and changes its CSS display property.

When should you use them?

  • Use v-if when a condition changes infrequently.
  • Use v-show when visibility changes frequently.

C. v-for

v-for is used to render lists.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const users = ref([
    { id: 1, name: 'Jalis' },
    { id: 2, name: 'Rahim' },
    { id: 3, name: 'Karim' }
])
</script>
<template>
    <ul>
        <li v-for="user in users" :key="user.id">
            {{ user.name }}
        </li>
    </ul>
</template>

The :key attribute helps Vue identify individual elements when updating a list.

Always use a stable, unique key whenever possible.

D. v-bind

v-bind dynamically binds HTML attributes to JavaScript values.

<script setup>
const imageUrl = '/images/product.png'
</script

<template>
    <img :src="imageUrl" alt="Product">
</template>

The shorthand for v-bind is :.

E. v-model

v-model creates two-way data binding between form inputs and JavaScript state.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const name = ref('')
</script>
<template>
    <input v-model="name" placeholder="Enter your name">
    <p>Hello, {{ name }}</p>
</template>

When the user types something, the reactive variable updates automatically.

6. Handling Events in Vue.js

Applications need to respond to user interactions.

For example:

  • Button clicks
  • Form submissions
  • Input changes
  • Mouse events
  • Keyboard events

Vue provides the v-on directive to handle events.

The shorthand is @.

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

Here, clicking the button executes the showMessage() function.

You can also use event modifiers:

<form @submit.prevent="submitForm">
    <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

const message = ref('')
const showMessage = () => {
    message.value = 'Button clicked successfully!'
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="showMessage">
        Click Me
    </button>
    <p>{{ message }}</p>
</template>

The .prevent modifier prevents the browser's default form submission behavior.

7. Understanding Computed Properties

Computed properties are useful when you need to calculate values based on reactive data.

Let’s imagine you have a product price and quantity.

Instead of calculating the total price repeatedly in your template, you can use computed().

<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'

const price = ref(100)
const quantity = ref(3)
const totalPrice = computed(() => {
    return price.value * quantity.value
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Price: {{ price }}</h2>
    <h2>Quantity: {{ quantity }}</h2>
    <h2>Total: {{ totalPrice }}</h2>
</template>

Whenever the price or quantity changes, Vue recalculates the computed value when needed.

Computed vs Methods

ComputedMethodsCached based on reactive dependenciesRuns whenever calledUseful for derived valuesUseful for actions and operationsRecalculates when dependencies changeExecutes on each invocation

Use computed properties for values derived from existing state.

8. Understanding Watchers

Sometimes you need to perform an action when a reactive value changes.

For this purpose, Vue provides watch().

Example:

<script setup>
import { ref, watch } from 'vue'

const search = ref('')
watch(search, (newValue, oldValue) => {
    console.log('New Search:', newValue)
    console.log('Previous Search:', oldValue)
})
</script>
<template>
    <input v-model="search" placeholder="Search products">
</template>

Whenever the search value changes, the watcher executes.

When Should You Use watch()?

  • Watching search input changes.
  • Calling an API after a filter changes.
  • Saving data when a setting changes.
  • Performing side effects based on reactive state.

Remember: Computed is generally for calculating values. Watch is for responding to changes with side effects.

9. Understanding Components in Vue.js

Components are reusable building blocks of Vue applications.

Imagine you are building an e-commerce website.

You might have:

  • Navbar
  • Product Card
  • Product List
  • Shopping Cart
  • Footer
  • Checkout Form

Instead of writing everything inside one large Vue file, you can create separate components.

Example:

ProductCard.vue

<script setup>
defineProps({
    name: String,
    price: Number
})
</script?

<template>
    <div class="product-card">
        <h3>{{ name }}</h3>
        <p>Price: {{ price }}</p>
    </div>
</template>

Now you can reuse this component multiple times.

<script setup>
import ProductCard from './components/ProductCard.vue'
</script>

<template>
    <ProductCard
        name="Keyboard"
        :price="1500"
    />
    <ProductCard
        name="Mouse"
        :price="800"
    />
</template>

This makes your application easier to maintain and scale.

10. Understanding Props and Emits

Props and Emits are important concepts in component communication.

A. Props

Props allow a parent component to pass data to a child component.

For example:

<ProductCard
    name="Keyboard"
    :price="1500"
/>

The child component receives these values through defineProps().

Props should be treated as read-only inside the child component.

B. Emits

Emits allow a child component to communicate with its parent by sending events.

Example:

<script setup>
const emit = defineEmits(['addToCart'])

const addProduct = () => {
    emit('addToCart', {
        id: 1,
        name: 'Keyboard'
    })
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="addProduct">
        Add to Cart
    </button>
</template>

The parent component can listen for the event:

<ProductCard @add-to-cart="handleAddToCart" />

This creates a clean communication pattern:

  • Props: Parent to Child
  • Emits: Child to Parent

11. Understanding Lifecycle Hooks

Every Vue component has a lifecycle.

A component is created, mounted, updated, and eventually unmounted.

Vue provides lifecycle hooks that allow developers to execute code at different stages.

Some commonly used lifecycle hooks are:

HookPurposeonMountedRuns after the component is mountedonUpdatedRuns after the component updatesonUnmountedRuns after the component is unmountedonBeforeMountRuns before mountingonBeforeUnmountRuns before unmounting

Example: onMounted()

<script setup>
import { onMounted } from 'vue'

onMounted(() => {
    console.log('Component mounted successfully!')
})
</script>
<template>
    <h2>Vue Lifecycle Example</h2>
</template>

A common use case is fetching initial data when a component loads.

<script setup>
import { ref, onMounted } from 'vue'

const users = ref([])
onMounted(async () => {
    const response = await fetch('/api/users')
    users.value = await response.json()
})
</script>

In production applications, you should also handle loading states, errors, and cancellation when appropriate.

12. Understanding Vue Router

When building a multi-page frontend application, you need a way to navigate between different pages without reloading the entire application.

Vue Router is the official routing solution for Vue.js.

For example, an e-commerce application might have:

  • / — Home page
  • /products — Product listing
  • /products/1 — Product details
  • /cart — Shopping cart
  • /checkout — Checkout page

A simple route configuration looks like this:

import { createRouter, createWebHistory } from 'vue-router'

import Home from './views/Home.vue'
import Products from './views/Products.vue'
const routes = [
    {
        path: '/',
        component: Home
    },
    {
        path: '/products',
        component: Products
    }
]
const router = createRouter({
    history: createWebHistory(),
    routes
})
export default router

You can then use:

<template>
    <router-link to="/">Home</router-link>

<router-link to="/products">Products</router-link>
    <router-view />
</template>

router-link handles navigation, while router-view displays the matched component.

13. Vue.js Composition API vs Options API

Vue supports two main styles of organizing component logic.

Options API

The Options API organizes component logic into options such as data, methods, computed, and lifecycle hooks.

<script>
export default {
    data() {
        return {
            count: 0
        }
    },
methods: {
        increment() {
            this.count++
        }
    }
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="increment">
        {{ count }}
    </button>
</template>

Composition API

The Composition API allows developers to organize logic using functions such as ref, computed, and watch.

<script setup>
import { ref } from 'vue'

const count = ref(0)
const increment = () => {
    count.value++
}
</script>
<template>
    <button @click="increment">
        {{ count }}
    </button>
</template>

Which One Should You Learn?

Both APIs are supported in Vue 3.

However, the Composition API with <script setup> is widely used in modern Vue 3 projects.

It also makes it easier to organize and reuse related logic through composables.

14. What Are Composables in Vue?

Composables are reusable functions that encapsulate reactive state and related logic.

They help developers avoid repeating the same logic across multiple components.

For example, imagine multiple components need access to the current user.

Instead of repeating the same logic everywhere, you can create a composable.

composables/useCounter.js

import { ref } from 'vue'

export function useCounter() {
    const count = ref(0)
    const increment = () => {
        count.value++
    }
    const decrement = () => {
        count.value--
    }
    return {
        count,
        increment,
        decrement
    }
}

Now use it inside a component:

<script setup>
import { useCounter } from './composables/useCounter'

const { count, increment, decrement } = useCounter()
</script>
<template>
    <h2>{{ count }}</h2>
    <button @click="increment">+</button>
    <button @click="decrement">-</button>
</template>

Composables are especially useful when building large applications with repeated frontend logic.

15. Best Practices for Vue.js Developers

Understanding Vue fundamentals is important, but writing clean and maintainable code is equally important.

Here are some practices worth following:

1. Build Reusable Components

Avoid writing your entire application inside one component.

2. Use Meaningful Component Names

Prefer ProductCard.vue instead of generic names such as Component1.vue.

3. Use Computed Properties for Derived Data

Avoid repeating complex calculations inside templates.

4. Use Stable Keys With v-for

Use unique identifiers instead of array indexes whenever possible.

5. Keep Components Focused

A component should have a clear responsibility.

6. Reuse Logic With Composables

Move reusable reactive logic into composable functions.

7. Handle API Errors Properly

Always consider loading states, validation errors, and failed requests.

8. Understand Reactivity Before Using State Libraries

Learn ref, reactive, computed, and watch before moving to more advanced state management tools.

16. What Should You Learn Next?

After understanding these fundamentals, you can gradually move toward more advanced Vue.js concepts.

Here is a suggested learning roadmap:

  1. JavaScript ES6+ fundamentals
  2. Vue 3 fundamentals
  3. Components, Props, and Emits
  4. Composition API
  5. Vue Router
  6. Pinia for state management
  7. API integration with Axios or Fetch
  8. Form validation
  9. Authentication and route protection
  10. Testing Vue components
  11. Performance optimization
  12. Building a complete project

Practice Project Ideas

Try building these projects to improve your understanding:

  • Todo Application
  • Weather Dashboard
  • Product Listing Page
  • Shopping Cart
  • Admin Dashboard
  • Inventory Management System

Building real projects will help you understand how individual Vue concepts work together.

Conclusion

Vue.js is a powerful yet approachable framework for building modern web interfaces.

Understanding its fundamentals is the first step toward becoming a better frontend developer.

Start with reactivity, directives, components, props, emits, and lifecycle hooks. Once you understand these concepts, you will find it much easier to build larger applications.

Don’t just memorize Vue syntax. Understand how data flows, how components communicate, and how reactivity works.

That’s how you move from writing Vue code to building real-world applications.

corrida_no_ar.resumo: Bernardo Fonseca, da X3M, discute a saturação dos formatos de corrida, a necessidade de inovação e como a mentalidade de suas expedições o ajuda a superar crises nos negócios. Ele também analisa o mercado de influenciadores e o papel da inteligência artificial no setor de…
corrida_no_ar.conteudo_html:
Domingo | 15 de novembro de 2026

No início de setembro, estive na TS Summit e bati um papo franco com Bernardo Fonseca, fundador da X3M. Falamos sobre o futuro das corridas de rua, a saturação dos formatos atuais, inovação, superação de crises, inteligência artificial e o mercado de influenciadores. Ele compartilhou sua visão sem filtros sobre os rumos do nosso esporte e como aplica a mentalidade de suas expedições extremas na gestão dos negócios.

Bernardo Fonseca aponta que, embora o mercado de corridas ainda esteja crescendo, o ritmo dessa expansão está diminuindo. Há alguns anos, o crescimento era de 45%, depois caiu para 25% e, mais recentemente, para 15%. Para ele, o problema não é a saturação do mercado em si, mas dos formatos tradicionais de 5k, 10k e maratonas, que já estão consolidados e com pouca margem para novidades. A solução, segundo ele, não é parar de criar eventos, mas sim mudar o formato. A “inquietude” de estar sempre se movimentando e buscando o novo é o que define o DNA da X3M.

Inovação, IA e a importância do autoral

A saída para a saturação, segundo Bernardo, é investir em produtos e “serviços autorais”, onde se tem domínio e controle sobre o que está sendo oferecido, em vez de apenas prestar um serviço padronizado. Ele também abordou o impacto da tecnologia, especialmente da Inteligência Artificial (IA). Para ele, a IA não é um diferencial, mas uma ferramenta que otimiza o trabalho. Bernardo fez uma analogia com a chegada do Excel para os contadores: a ferramenta não substituiu o profissional, mas um contador que usa o computador e o Excel é muito mais eficiente do que um que usa apenas a calculadora.
